title: Bill Russell on the word jazz, its New Orleans origin and reading music
summary: Russell says the name jazz came in Chicago, older musicians said ragtime, the music started in New Orleans, and many early players read music.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Oh, you have the drawing.
Where did the name jazz start?

No, that's another thing a lot of people have been talking and arguing about for years. Actually, it seems the name jazz has applied to the music, wasn't used with the music until it got to Chicago, probably, as far as we know. Although sometimes you'll find people down here that'll claim they maybe heard the word used in connection with music and somebody will dig it up as being used, oh, way back, oh, 50 years before anybody ever heard of a jazz band and all of that. But to me, the name has never been important. I never even think about it. Most of the music, older musicians here will call it ragtime. They'll talk about the ragtime bands and they just think of it as the music, the dance music that they played.
Well, how did this all start? Does it really have a unique start here in New Orleans?

To me, as far as I've been able to discover, I think the type of music that we call jazz today and this American dance music, what might be called the hotter variety, the more improvised form of it, as far as I've been able to determine, it really did start here.
Most of these musicians don't know how to read music, though, do they?

Well, no, I wouldn't say that. I'd say probably at least half of them have. Even the best ones. If you, all the way back to the 1890s even. Probably more of them in the beginning knew how to read music than some of the musicians today.
